pages.text: Every Saturday, Ewurama helped her aunt, Maa Gifty, sell tomatoes at the market stall. Today Maa Gifty sighed as she sorted the basket. ‘Another ten tomatoes gone soft,’ she said. ‘I cannot sell those.’
sentences: Every Saturday, Ewurama helped her aunt, Maa Gifty, sell tomatoes at the market stall.
Today Maa Gifty sighed as she sorted the basket.
‘Another ten tomatoes gone soft,’ she said.
‘I cannot sell those.’
pages.alt: A girl and her aunt sort tomatoes at a busy market stall; some soft tomatoes are set aside.

pages.text: Ewurama and her friend Issah decided to find out why. ‘A good detective starts with one clear question,’ said Issah. ‘Ours: do tomatoes spoil faster in the sun or in the shade?’
sentences: Ewurama and her friend Issah decided to find out why.
‘A good detective starts with one clear question,’ said Issah.
‘Ours: do tomatoes spoil faster in the sun or in the shade?’
pages.alt: Two children huddle over a notebook beside the stall, with a basket of tomatoes.

pages.text: On Monday, they chose six firm tomatoes of the same size. They put three on a plate in the sunny yard and three on a plate under the shed. They wrote the date in their notebook.
sentences: On Monday, they chose six firm tomatoes of the same size.
They put three on a plate in the sunny yard and three on a plate under the shed.
They wrote the date in their notebook.
pages.alt: Two plates of tomatoes sit in a sunny yard and in a shaded shed, with a notebook beside them.

pages.text: Each day they looked, touched gently and drew pictures. On day two, the sunny tomatoes looked wrinkled. By day four, one had a soft, brown patch. The shaded tomatoes still looked smooth.
sentences: Each day they looked, touched gently and drew pictures.
On day two, the sunny tomatoes looked wrinkled.
By day four, one had a soft, brown patch.
The shaded tomatoes still looked smooth.
pages.alt: Two children draw tomatoes at different stages next to the plates.

pages.text: ‘Maybe we were just unlucky,’ said Issah. ‘One test is not enough.’ Ewurama agreed. They repeated the test with six new tomatoes and found the same pattern.
sentences: ‘Maybe we were just unlucky,’ said Issah.
‘One test is not enough.’ Ewurama agreed.
They repeated the test with six new tomatoes and found the same pattern.
pages.alt: The children set out two new plates of tomatoes and write in the notebook.

pages.text: They showed Maa Gifty their notebook. ‘So I should keep my tomatoes in the shade?’ she asked. ‘We have not tested everything,’ said Ewurama. ‘A damp cloth is our next experiment.’
sentences: They showed Maa Gifty their notebook.
‘So I should keep my tomatoes in the shade?’ she asked.
‘We have not tested everything,’ said Ewurama.
‘A damp cloth is our next experiment.’
pages.alt: The aunt reads the children’s notebook at her stall, smiling.

pages.text: Maa Gifty moved her baskets under the umbrella and used crates with gaps for air. After two weeks, she threw away fewer tomatoes. ‘That saves food, and it saves me money,’ she said.
sentences: Maa Gifty moved her baskets under the umbrella and used crates with gaps for air.
After two weeks, she threw away fewer tomatoes.
‘That saves food, and it saves me money,’ she said.
pages.alt: Tomatoes in open crates are shaded by an umbrella at the market stall.

pages.text: Ewurama wrote in the notebook: ‘We do not know everything about why tomatoes spoil. But our test gave us one useful answer, and now we know our next question.’ The end.
sentences: Ewurama wrote in the notebook: ‘We do not know everything about why tomatoes spoil.
But our test gave us one useful answer, and now we know our next question.’ The end.
